sections.h: The flood in Atrahasis, Tablet III
sections.b:
The oldest dated tablets of a Babylonian flood story, as Alexander Heidel noted, are the copies of Atrahasis made in the reign of Ammi-saduqa, king of Babylon (Heidel, p. 261). Tablet III, the flood, was copied by the scribe Ipiq-Aya at Sippar in that king's twelfth year (SEAL). Enki warns Atrahasis by speaking to his reed wall, because the gods have sworn an oath; Atrahasis builds a boat with the help of his unknowing town, loads animals and his family, and seals the door as Adad thunders. The storm lasts seven days and seven nights. The gods themselves are terrified and starving, and the mother goddess weeps for her children floating like dragonflies. Afterward the gods crowd "like flies" over his offering, Enlil rages that a man survived, and Enki decrees limits on human births instead of floods.

Many elements are shared with Genesis 6-9: warning, vessel, animals, family, door, storm, offering, divine smelling, a sign in heaven tied to remembering. After the flood the order differs (see the Atrahasis chapter 12 page), and the meaning runs the other way: in Genesis one just God both judges and saves, warns openly, needs no food, and answers the offering with a covenant and a blessing to fill the earth.

sections.h: Other old versions: the Ark Tablet, Nippur, Ugarit
sections.b: Fragments of other versions add details. The Ark Tablet (SEAL files it with the Middle Babylonian copies) draws the boat as a huge round coracle and says the wild animals went in "two by two." A Middle Babylonian piece from Nippur calls the boat "Preserver of Life." A copy from Ugarit has the hero call himself an anointed priest who lives in the house of Ea. The Babylonian priest Berossus, writing in Greek, keeps the dream warning, the boat, birds sent out three times and an altar on the mountain.

common: Alexander Heidel judged it "too obvious to require proof" that the Babylonian and Hebrew flood stories are genetically related (1949), and A. R. Millard, from a believing standpoint, held that both "undoubtedly describe the same Flood" (1967).
uncommon: A. R. Millard argued that borrowing by Genesis "has yet to be shown," and that both remember one real flood, with Genesis the more probable account.

sections.h: Atrahasis, Utnapishtim, Ziusudra: the Babylonian Noah
sections.b: The hero of the Mesopotamian flood has several names: Atrahasis, "exceedingly wise" (or, as Millard suggested, "exceedingly devout"); Utnapishtim in the Epic of Gilgamesh, which also calls him Atrahasis; Ziusudra in the Sumerian Flood Story; Xisuthros in Berossus. Like Noah he is warned, builds a vessel, saves his family and the animals, and offers sacrifice. Unlike Noah he is warned in secret by one god against the others, and he hides the warning from his neighbors with a cover story, while Noah is a "herald of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5). Millard held that the Babylonian and biblical accounts "undoubtedly describe the same Flood"; he does not say more about the man. The site's own verdict, from its Christian standpoint, is that Atrahasis is very likely Noah as the Babylonians remembered him (see the book's "Who's who"), while the names, the rank of the hero and the way he is saved do not match.

sections.h: Hungry gods and a soothing smell
sections.b: In Atrahasis humans exist to feed the gods. The flood leaves the gods "thirsty and starving" (11:29), and when Atrahasis makes his offering they smell it and crowd "like flies" over it and eat (12:7-9). Genesis keeps the smell, "The LORD smelled the soothing smell" (Genesis 8:21), but drops the hunger: God answers with a promise for the earth. The Psalms deny outright that God feeds on offerings (Psalm 50:12-13), and Paul says Christ gave himself "a soothing smell" to God (Ephesians 5:2).

After the flood in Atrahasis, the god Enki decrees that among humans there will be "women who give birth and women who do not," a demon to snatch infants, and priestesses forbidden to bear children (12:68-76). Tikva Frymer-Kensky read these as the gods' permanent answer to overpopulation. The Bible tells the opposite story: God blesses Noah's family, "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth" (Genesis 9:1), and barren women such as Sarah and Hannah become mothers by his gift (Psalm 113:9).

In Atrahasis the gods regret the flood as a mistake: the mother goddess cannot believe she voted for "total destruction" and blames Enlil, who "did not think it through" (11:34-37, 11:51; 12:15). In Genesis the LORD is pained over human evil before the flood (Genesis 6:6), and after it he does not call the judgment a mistake but binds himself by covenant never to flood the earth again (Genesis 9:11).
